entries.840cbb991216473643e05fcaaddaade65c749c93: <div sID="gen5684" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="20" osisID="1Sam.20" sID="1Sam.20"/> <div eID="gen5684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5685" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5686" type="x-p"/> David, having several times narrowly escaped Saul's fury, begins to consider at last whether it may not be necessary for him to retire into the country and to take up arms in his own defence. But he will not do so daring a thing without consulting his faithful friend Jonathan; how he did this, and what passed between them, we have an account in this chapter, where we have as surprising instances of supernatural love as we had in the chapter before of unnatural hatred. I. David complains to Jonathan of his present distress, and engages him to be his friend, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.1-1Sam.20.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. II. Jonathan faithfully promises to get and give him intelligence how his father stood affected to him, and renews the covenant of friendship with him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.9-1Sam.20.23">ver. 9-23</reference>. III. Jonathan, upon trial, finds, to his grief, that his father was implacably enraged against David, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.24-1Sam.20.34">ver. 24-34</reference>. IV. He gives David notice of this, according to the appointment between them, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.35-1Sam.20.42">ver. 35-42</reference>.
entries.5521aca382e16276493702cb6a476001b468b006: <div eID="gen5686" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5685" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David Consults Jonathan. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1058.)</title> <div sID="gen5687" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And David fled from Naioth in Ramah, and came and said before Jonathan, What have I done? what <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine iniquity? and what <hi type="italic">is</hi> my sin before thy father, that he seeketh my life? <hi type="super">2</hi> And he said unto him, God forbid; thou shalt not die: behold, my father will do nothing either great or small, but that he will shew it me: and why should my father hide this thing from me? it <hi type="italic">is</hi> not <hi type="italic">so.</hi> <hi type="super">3</hi> And David sware moreover, and said, Thy father certainly knoweth that I have found grace in thine eyes; and he saith, Let not Jonathan know this, lest he be grieved: but truly <hi type="italic">as</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth, and <hi type="italic">as</hi> thy soul liveth, <hi type="italic">there is</hi> but a step between me and death. <hi type="super">4</hi> Then said Jonathan unto David, Whatsoever thy soul desireth, I will even do <hi type="italic">it</hi> for thee. <hi type="super">5</hi> And David said unto Jonathan, Behold, to morrow <hi type="italic">is</hi> the new moon, and I should not fail to sit with the king at meat: but let me go, that I may hide myself in the field unto the third <hi type="italic">day</hi> at even. <hi type="super">6</hi> If thy father at all miss me, then say, David earnestly asked <hi type="italic">leave</hi> of me that he might run to Bethlehem his city: for <hi type="italic">there is</hi> a yearly sacrifice there for all the family. <hi type="super">7</hi> If he say thus, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> well; thy servant shall have peace: but if he be very wroth, <hi type="italic">then</hi> be sure that evil is determined by him. <hi type="super">8</hi> Therefore thou shalt deal kindly with thy servant; for thou hast brought thy servant into a covenant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> with thee: notwithstanding, if there be in me iniquity, slay me thyself; for why shouldest thou bring me to thy father? <div eID="gen5687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5688" type="x-p"/> Here, I. David makes a representation to Jonathan of his present troubles. While Saul lay bound by his trance at Naioth David escaped to the court, and got to speak with Jonathan. And it was happy for him that he had such a friend at court, when he had such an enemy on the throne. If there be those that hate and despise us, let us not be disturbed at that, for there are those also that love and respect us. God hath set the one over against the other, and so must we. Jonathan was a friend that loved at all times, loved David as well now in his distress, and bade him as welcome into his arms, as he had done when he was in his triumph (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.1">ch. xviii. 1</reference>), and he was <hi type="italic">a brother that was born for adversity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.17">Prov. xvii. 17</reference>. Now, 1. David appeals to Jonathan himself concerning his innocency, and he needed not say much to him for the proof of it, only he desired him that if he knew of any just offence he had given his father he would tell him, that he might humble himself and beg his pardon: <hi type="italic">What have I done?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.1">v. 1</reference>. 2. He endeavors to convince him that, notwithstanding his innocency, Saul sought his life. Jonathan, from a principal of filial respect to his father, was very loth to believe that he designed or would ever do so wicked a thing, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.2">v. 2</reference>. He the rather hoped so because he knew nothing of any such design, and he had usually been made privy to all his counsels. Jonathan, as became a dutiful son, endeavored to cover his father's shame, as far as was consistent with justice and fidelity to David. Charity is not forward to think evil of any, especially of a parent, <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.5">1 Cor. xiii. 5</reference>. David therefore gives him the assurance of an oath concerning his own danger, swears the peace upon Saul, that he was in fear of his life by him: "<hi type="italic">As the Lord liveth,</hi> than which nothing more sure in itself, and as <hi type="italic">thy soul liveth,</hi> than which nothing more certain to thee, whatever thou thinkest, <hi type="italic">there is but a step between me and death,</hi>" <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.3">v. 3</reference>. And, as for Saul's concealing it from Jonathan, it was easy to account for that; he knew the friendship between him and David, and therefore, though in other things he advised with him, yet not in that. None more fit than Jonathan to serve him in every design that was just and honourable, but he knew him to be a man of more virtue than to be his confidant in so base a design as the murder of David. <div eID="gen5688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5689" type="x-p"/> II. Jonathan generously offers him his service (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Whatsoever thou desirest,</hi> he needed not insert the proviso of lawful and honest (for he knew David too well to think he would ask any thing that was otherwise), <hi type="italic">I will even do it for thee.</hi> This is true friendship. Thus Christ testifies his love to us: <hi type="italic">Ask, and it shall be done for you;</hi> and we must testify ours to him by keeping his commandments. <div eID="gen5689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5690" type="x-p"/> III. David only desires him to satisfy himself, and then to satisfy him whether Saul did really design his death or no. Perhaps David proposed this more for Jonathan's conviction than his own, for he himself was well satisfied. 1. The method of trial he proposed was very natural, and would certainly discover how Saul stood affected to him. The two next days Saul was to dine publicly, upon occasion of the solemnities of the new moon, when extraordinary sacrifices were offered and feasts made upon the sacrifices. Saul was rejected of God, and the Spirit of the Lord had departed from him, yet he kept up his observance of the holy feasts. There may be the remains of external devotion where there is nothing but the ruins of real virtue. At these solemn feasts Saul had either all his children to sit with him, and David had a seat as one of them, or all his great officers, and David had a seat as one of <hi type="italic">them.</hi> However it was, David resolved his seat should be empty (and that it never used to be at a sacred feast) those two days (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.5">v. 5</reference>), and he would abscond till the solemnity was over, and put it upon this issue: if Saul admitted an excuse for his absence, and dispensed with it, he would conclude he had changed his mind and was reconciled to him; but if he resented it, and was put into a passion by it, it was easy to conclude he designed him a mischief, since it was certain he did not love him so well as to desire his presence for any other end than that he might have an opportunity to do him a mischief, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.7">v. 7</reference>. 2. The excuse he desired Jonathan to make for his absence, we have reason to think, was true, that he was invited by his elder brother to Bethlehem, his own city, to celebrate this new moon with his relations there, because, besides the monthly solemnity in which they held communion with all Israel, they had now a yearly sacrifice, and a holy feast upon it, for <hi type="italic">all the family,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.6">v. 6</reference>. They kept a day of thanksgiving in their family for the comforts they enjoyed, and of prayer for the continuance of them. By this it appears that the family David was of was a very religious family, a house that had a church in it. 3. The arguments he used with Jonathan to persuade him to do this kindness for him were very pressing, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.8">v. 8</reference>. (1.) That he had entered into a league of friendship with him, and it was Jonathan's own proposal: <hi type="italic">Thou hast brought thy servant into a covenant of the Lord with thee.</hi> (2.) That he would by no means urge him to espouse his cause if he was not sure that it was a righteous cause: "<hi type="italic">If there be iniquity in me,</hi> I am so far from desiring or expecting that the covenant between us should bind thee to be a confederate with me in that iniquity that I freely release thee from it, and wish that my hand may be first upon me: <hi type="italic">Slay me thyself.</hi>" No honest man will urge his friend to do a dishonest thing for his sake.
entries.38751106a17589ad14c915d804ffba5a021a5c97: <div eID="gen5690" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jonathan's Covenant with David. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1058.)</title> <div sID="gen5691" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And Jonathan said, Far be it from thee: for if I knew certainly that evil were determined by my father to come upon thee, then would not I tell it thee? <hi type="super">10</hi> Then said David to Jonathan, Who shall tell me? or what <hi type="italic">if</hi> thy father answer thee roughly? <hi type="super">11</hi> And Jonathan said unto David, Come, and let us go out into the field. And they went out both of them into the field. <hi type="super">12</hi> And Jonathan said unto David, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> God of Israel, when I have sounded my father about to morrow any time, <hi type="italic">or</hi> the third <hi type="italic">day,</hi> and, behold, <hi type="italic">if there be</hi> good toward David, and I then send not unto thee, and shew it thee; <hi type="super">13</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> do so and much more to Jonathan: but if it please my father <hi type="italic">to do</hi> thee evil, then I will shew it thee, and send thee away, that thou mayest go in peace: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> be with thee, as he hath been with my father. <hi type="super">14</hi> And thou shalt not only while yet I live shew me the kindness of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that I die not: <hi type="super">15</hi> But <hi type="italic">also</hi> thou shalt not cut off thy kindness from my house for ever: no, not when the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath cut off the enemies of David every one from the face of the earth. <hi type="super">16</hi> So Jonathan made <hi type="italic">a covenant</hi> with the house of David, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> Let the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> even require <hi type="italic">it</hi> at the hand of David's enemies. <hi type="super">17</hi> And Jonathan caused David to swear again, because he loved him: for he loved him as he loved his own soul. <hi type="super">18</hi> Then Jonathan said to David, To morrow <hi type="italic">is</hi> the new moon: and thou shalt be missed, because thy seat will be empty. <hi type="super">19</hi> And <hi type="italic">when</hi> thou hast stayed three days, <hi type="italic">then</hi> thou shalt go down quickly, and come to the place where thou didst hide thyself when the business was <hi type="italic">in hand,</hi> and shalt remain by the stone Ezel. <hi type="super">20</hi> And I will shoot three arrows on the side <hi type="italic">thereof,</hi> as though I shot at a mark. <hi type="super">21</hi> And, behold, I will send a lad, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> Go, find out the arrows. If I expressly say unto the lad, Behold, the arrows <hi type="italic">are</hi> on this side of thee, take them; then come thou: for <hi type="italic">there is</hi> peace to thee, and no hurt; <hi type="italic">as</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth. <hi type="super">22</hi> But if I say thus unto the young man, Behold, the arrows <hi type="italic">are</hi> beyond thee; go thy way: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath sent thee away. <hi type="super">23</hi> And <hi type="italic">as touching</hi> the matter which thou and I have spoken of, behold, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">be</hi> between thee and me for ever. <div eID="gen5691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5692" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Jonathan protests his fidelity to David in his distress. Notwithstanding the strong confidence David had in Jonathan, yet, because he might have some reason to fear that his father's influence, and his own interest, should make him warp, or grow cool towards him, Jonathan thought it requisite solemnly to renew the professions of his friendship to him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Far be it from thee</hi> to think that I suspect thee of any crime for which I should either slay thee myself or deliver thee to my father; no, if thou hast any jealousy of that, <hi type="italic">Come let us go into the field</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.11">v. 11</reference>), and talk it over more fully." He did not challenge him to the field to fight him for an affront, but to fix him in his friendship. He faithfully promised him that he would let him know how, upon trial, he found his father affected towards him, and would make the matter neither better nor worse than it was. "If there be <hi type="italic">good towards thee,</hi> I will <hi type="italic">show it thee,</hi> that thou mayest be easy (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.12">v. 12</reference>), if evil, I will <hi type="italic">send thee away,</hi> that thou mayest be safe" (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.13">v. 13</reference>); and thus he would help to deliver him from the evil if it were real and from the fear of evil if it were but imaginary. For the confirmation of his promise he appeals to God, 1. As a witness (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">O Lord God of Israel,</hi> thou knowest I mean sincerely, and think as I speak." The strength of his passion made the manner of his speaking concise and abrupt. 2. As a judge: "<hi type="italic">The Lord do so and much more to Jonathan</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.13">v. 13</reference>), if I speak deceitfully, or break my word with my friend." He expressed himself thus solemnly that David might be abundantly assured of his sincerity. And thus God has confirmed his promises to us, that we might have <hi type="italic">strong consolation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.6.17-Heb.6.18">Heb. vi. 17, 18</reference>. Jonathan adds to his protestations his hearty prayers: "<hi type="italic">The Lord be with thee,</hi> to protect and prosper thee, <hi type="italic">as he has been</hi> formerly <hi type="italic">with my father,</hi> though now he has withdrawn." Thus he imitates his belief that David would be in his father's place, and his good wishes that he might prosper in it better than his father now did. <div eID="gen5692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5693" type="x-p"/> II. He provides for the entail of the covenant of friendship with David upon his posterity, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.14-1Sam.20.16">v. 14-16</reference>. He engages David to be a friend to his family when he was gone (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt</hi> promise that thou wilt <hi type="italic">not cut off thy kindness from my house for ever.</hi> This he spoke from a natural affection he had to his children, whom he desired it might go well with after his decease, and for whose future welfare he desired to improve his present interest. It also intimates his firm belief of David's advancement, and that it would be in the power of his hand to do a kindness or unkindness to his seed; for, in process of time, <hi type="italic">the Lord would cut off his enemies,</hi> Saul himself was not expected; then "<hi type="italic">Do not thou cut off thy kindness from my house,</hi> nor revenge my father's wrongs upon my children." The house of David must likewise be bound to the house of Jonathan from generation to generation; he <hi type="italic">made a covenant</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.16">v. 16</reference>) <hi type="italic">with the house of David.</hi> Note, True friends cannot but covet to transmit to theirs after them their mutual affections. <hi type="italic">Thy own friend, and thy father's friend, forsake not.</hi> This kindness, 1. He calls <hi type="italic">the kindness of the Lord,</hi> because it is such kindness as God shows to those he takes into covenant with himself; for he is a God to them and to their seed; they are <hi type="italic">beloved for the fathers' sakes.</hi> 2. He secures it by an imprecation (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord require it at the hand of David's seed</hi> (for of David himself he had no suspicion) if they prove so far David's enemies as to deal wrongfully with the posterity of Jonathan, David's friend. He feared lest David, or some of his, should hereafter be tempted, for the clearing and confirming of their title to the throne, to do by his seed as Abimelech had done by the sons of Gideon (<reference osisRef="Judg.9.5">Judg. ix. 5</reference>), and this he would effectually prevent; but the reason given (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.17">v. 17</reference>) why Jonathan was so earnest to have the friendship entailed is purely generous, and has nothing of self in it; it was because <hi type="italic">he loved him as he loved his own soul,</hi> and therefore desired that he and his might be beloved by him. David, though now in disgrace at court and in distress, was as amiable in the eyes of Jonathan as ever he had been, and he loved him never the less for his father's hating him, so pure were the principles on which his friendship was built. Having himself sworn to David, he caused David to swear to him, and (as we read it) <hi type="italic">to swear again,</hi> which David consented to (for he that bears an honest mind does not startle at assurances), to swear by his love to him, which he looked upon as a sacred thing. Jonathan's heart was so much upon it that, when they parted this time, he concluded with a solemn appeal to God: <hi type="italic">The Lord be between me and thee for ever</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.23">v. 23</reference>), that is, "God himself be judge between us and our families for ever, if on either side this league of friendship be violated." It was in remembrance of this covenant that David was kind to Mephibosheth, <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.7">2 Sam. ix. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.7">xxi. 7</reference>. It will be a kindness to ourselves and ours to secure an interest in those whom God favours and to make his friends ours. <div eID="gen5693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5694" type="x-p"/> III. He settles the method of intelligence, and by what signs and tokens he would give him notice how his father stood affected towards him. David would be missed the first day, or at least the second day, of the new moon, and would be enquired after, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.18">v. 18</reference>. On the third day, by which time he would have returned from Bethlehem, he must be at such a place (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.19">v. 19</reference>), and Jonathan would come towards that place with his bow and arrows to shoot for diversion (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.20">v. 20</reference>), would send his lad to fetch his arrows, and, if they were shot short of the lad, David must take it for a signal of safety, and not be afraid to show his head (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.21">v. 21</reference>); but, if he shot beyond the lad, it was a signal of danger, and he must shift for his safety, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.22">v. 22</reference>. This expedient he fixed lest he should not have the opportunity, which yet it proved he had, of talking with David, and making the report by word of mouth.
entries.ce2ae8bfb1387e8690aff8e4cc61d9949e592498: <div eID="gen5694" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jonathan Excuses David to Saul. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1058.)</title> <div sID="gen5695" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> So David hid himself in the field: and when the new moon was come, the king sat him down to eat meat. <hi type="super">25</hi> And the king sat upon his seat, as at other times, <hi type="italic">even</hi> upon a seat by the wall: and Jonathan arose, and Abner sat by Saul's side, and David's place was empty. <hi type="super">26</hi> Nevertheless Saul spake not any thing that day: for he thought, Something hath befallen him, he <hi type="italic">is</hi> not clean; surely he <hi type="italic">is</hi> not clean. <hi type="super">27</hi> And it came to pass on the morrow, <hi type="italic">which was</hi> the second <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, that David's place was empty: and Saul said unto Jonathan his son, Wherefore cometh not the son of Jesse to meat, neither yesterday, nor to day? <hi type="super">28</hi> And Jonathan answered Saul, David earnestly asked <hi type="italic">leave</hi> of me <hi type="italic">to go</hi> to Bethlehem: <hi type="super">29</hi> And he said, Let me go, I pray thee; for our family hath a sacrifice in the city; and my brother, he hath commanded me <hi type="italic">to be there:</hi> and now, if I have found favour in thine eyes, let me get away, I pray thee, and see my brethren. Therefore he cometh not unto the king's table. <hi type="super">30</hi> Then Saul's anger was kindled against Jonathan, and he said unto him, Thou son of the perverse rebellious <hi type="italic">woman,</hi> do not I know that thou hast chosen the son of Jesse to thine own confusion, and unto the confusion of thy mother's nakedness? <hi type="super">31</hi> For as long as the son of Jesse liveth upon the ground, thou shalt not be established, nor thy kingdom. Wherefore now send and fetch him unto me, for he shall surely die. <hi type="super">32</hi> And Jonathan answered Saul his father, and said unto him, Wherefore shall he be slain? what hath he done? <hi type="super">33</hi> And Saul cast a javelin at him to smite him: whereby Jonathan knew that it was determined of his father to slay David. <hi type="super">34</hi> So Jonathan arose from the table in fierce anger, and did eat no meat the second day of the month: for he was grieved for David, because his father had done him shame. <div eID="gen5695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5696" type="x-p"/> Jonathan is here effectually convinced of that which he was so loth to believe, that his father had an implacable enmity to David, and would certainly be the death of him if it were in his power; and he had like to have paid very dearly himself for the conviction. <div eID="gen5696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5697" type="x-p"/> I. David is missed from the feast on the first day, but nothing is said of him. <hi type="italic">The king sat upon his seat,</hi> to feast upon the peace-offerings <hi type="italic">as at other times</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.25">v. 25</reference>), and yet had his heart as full of envy and malice against David as it could hold. He should first have been reconciled to him, and then have come and offered his gift; but, instead of that, he hoped, at this feast, to drink the blood of David. What an abomination was that sacrifice which was brought with such a wicked mind as this! <reference osisRef="Prov.21.27">Prov. xxi. 27</reference>. When the king came to take his seat Jonathan arose, in reverence to him both as a father and as his sovereign; every one knew his place, but David's was empty. It did not use to be so. None more content than he in attending holy duties; nor had he been absent now but that he must have come at the peril of his life; self-preservation obliged him to withdraw. In imminent peril present opportunities may be waived, nay, we ought not to throw ourselves into the mouth of danger. Christ him self absconded often, till he knew that his hour had come. But that day Saul took no notice that he missed David, but said within himself, "<hi type="italic">Surely he is not clean,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.26">v. 26</reference>. Some ceremonial pollution has befallen him, which forbids him to eat of the holy things till he has <hi type="italic">washed his clothes, and bathed his flesh in water, and been unclean until the evening.</hi>" Saul knew what conscience David made of the law, and that he would rather keep away from the holy feast than come in his uncleanness. Blessed be God, no uncleanness is now a restraint upon us, but what we may by faith and repentance be washed from in the fountain opened, <reference osisRef="Ps.26.6">Ps. xxvi. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen5697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5698" type="x-p"/> II. He is enquired for the second day, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.27">v. 27</reference>. Saul asked Jonathan, who he knew was his confidant, <hi type="italic">Wherefore cometh not the son of Jesse to meat?</hi> He was his own son by marriage, but he calls him in disdain, <hi type="italic">the son of Jesse.</hi> He asks for him as if he were not pleased that he should be absent from a religious feast; and so it should be example to masters of families to see to it that those under their charge be not absent from the worship of God, either in public or in the family. It is a bad thing for us, except in case of necessity, to omit an opportunity of statedly attending on God in solemn ordinances. Thomas lost a sight of Christ by being once absent from a meeting of the disciples. But that which displeased Saul was that hereby he missed the opportunity he expected of doing David a mischief. <div eID="gen5698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5699" type="x-p"/> III. Jonathan makes his excuse, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.28-1Sam.20.29">v. 28, 29</reference>. 1. That he was absent upon a good occasion, keeping the feast in another place, though not here, sent for by his elder brother, who was now more respectful to him than he had been (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.28">ch. xvii. 28</reference>), and that he had gone to pay his respects to his relations, for the keeping up of brotherly love; and no master would deny a servant liberty to do that in due time. He pleads, 2. That he did not go without leave humbly asked and obtained from Jonathan, who, as his superior officer, was proper to be applied to for it. Thus he represents David as not wanting in any instance of respect and duty to the government. <div eID="gen5699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5700" type="x-p"/> IV. Saul hereupon breaks out into a most extravagant passion, and rages like a lion disappointed of his prey. David was out of his reach, but he falls upon Jonathan for his sake (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.30-1Sam.20.31">v. 30, 31</reference>), gives him base language, not fit for a gentleman, a prince, to give to any man, especially his own son, heir apparent to his crown, a son that served him, the greatest stay and ornament of his family, before a great deal of company, at a feast, when all should be in good humour, at a sacred feast, by which all irregular passions should be mortified and subdued; yet he does in effect call him, 1. A bastard: <hi type="italic">Thou son of the perverse rebellious woman;</hi> that is, according to the foolish filthy language of men's brutish passion now a day, "Thou son of a whore." He tells him he was born <hi type="italic">to the confusion of his mother,</hi> that is, he had given the world cause to suspect that he was not the legitimate son of Saul, because he loved him whom Saul hated and supported him who would be the destruction of their family. 2. A traitor: <hi type="italic">Thou son of a perverse rebellion</hi> (so the word is), that is, "thou perverse rebel." At other times he reckoned no counsellor or commander that he had more trusty and well-beloved than Jonathan; yet now in this passion he represents him as dangerous to his crown and life. 3. A fool: <hi type="italic">Thou hast chosen the son of Jesse</hi> for thy friend <hi type="italic">to thy own confusion,</hi> for while he lives <hi type="italic">thou shalt never be established.</hi> Jonathan indeed did wisely and well for himself and family to secure an interest in David, whom Heaven had destined to the throne, yet, for this, he is branded as most impolitic. It is good taking God's people for our people and going with those that have him with them. It will prove to our advantage at last, however for the present it may be thought a disparagement, and a prejudice to our secular interest. It is probable Saul knew that David was anointed to the kingdom by the same hand that anointed him, and then not Jonathan, but himself, was the fool, to think to defeat the counsels of God. Yet nothing will serve him but David must die, and Jonathan must fetch him to execution. See how ill Saul's passion looks, and let it warn us against the indulgence of any thing like it in ourselves. Anger is madness, and <hi type="italic">he that hates his brother is a murderer.</hi> <div eID="gen5700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5701" type="x-p"/> V. Jonathan is sorely grieved and put into disorder by his father's barbarous passion, and the more because he had hoped better things, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.2">v. 2</reference>. He was troubled for his father, that he should be such a brute, troubled for his friend, whom he knew to be a friend of God, that he should be so basely abused; he was <hi type="italic">grieved for David</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.34">v. 34</reference>), and troubled for himself too, because <hi type="italic">his father had done him shame,</hi> and, though most unjustly, yet he must submit to it. One would pity Jonathan to see how he was put, 1. Into the peril of sin. Much ado that wise and good man had to keep his temper, upon such a provocation as this. His father's reflections upon himself made no return to; it becomes inferiors to bear with meekness and silence the contempts put upon them in wrath and passion. <hi type="italic">When thou art the anvil lie thou still.</hi> But his dooming David to die he could not bear: to that he replied with some heat (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.32">v. 32</reference>), <hi type="italic">Wherefore shall he be slain?</hi> <hi type="italic">What has he done?</hi> Generous spirits can much more easily bear to be abused themselves than to hear their friends abused. 2. Into the peril of death. Saul was now so outrageous that he threw his javelin at Jonathan, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.33">v. 33</reference>. He seemed to be in great care (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.31">v. 31</reference>) than Jonathan should be established in his kingdom, and yet now he himself aims at his life. What fools, what savage beasts and worse does anger make men! How necessary it is to put a hook in its nose and a bridle in its jaws! Jonathan was fully satisfied that evil was determined against David, which put him out of frame exceedingly: he <hi type="italic">rose from table,</hi> thinking it high time when his life was struck at, and <hi type="italic">would eat no meat,</hi> for they were not to eat of the holy things in their mourning. All the guests, we may suppose, were discomposed, and the mirth of the feast was spoiled. <hi type="italic">He that is cruel troubles his own flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.11.17">Prov. xi. 17</reference>.
entries.700c308609f2d368b1dbd6d789d0a0bd5a2137ed: <div eID="gen5701" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Informed of His Danger. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1058.)</title> <div sID="gen5702" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">35</hi> And it came to pass in the morning, that Jonathan went out into the field at the time appointed with David, and a little lad with him. <hi type="super">36</hi> And he said unto his lad, Run, find out now the arrows which I shoot. <hi type="italic">And</hi> as the lad ran, he shot an arrow beyond him. <hi type="super">37</hi> And when the lad was come to the place of the arrow which Jonathan had shot, Jonathan cried after the lad, and said, <hi type="italic">Is</hi> not the arrow beyond thee? <hi type="super">38</hi> And Jonathan cried after the lad, Make speed, haste, stay not. And Jonathan's lad gathered up the arrows, and came to his master. <hi type="super">39</hi> But the lad knew not any thing: only Jonathan and David knew the matter. <hi type="super">40</hi> And Jonathan gave his artillery unto his lad, and said unto him, Go, carry <hi type="italic">them</hi> to the city. <hi type="super">41</hi> <hi type="italic">And</hi> as soon as the lad was gone, David arose out of <hi type="italic">a place</hi> toward the south, and fell on his face to the ground, and bowed himself three times: and they kissed one another, and wept one with another, until David exceeded. <hi type="super">42</hi> And Jonathan said to David, Go in peace, forasmuch as we have sworn both of us in the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> be between me and thee, and between my seed and thy seed for ever. And he arose and departed: and Jonathan went into the city. <div eID="gen5702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5703" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. Jonathan's faithful performance of his promise to give David notice of the success of his dangerous experiment. He went at the time and to the place appointed (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.35">v. 35</reference>), within sight of which he knew David lay hid, sent his footboy to fetch his arrows, which he would shoot at random (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.36">v. 36</reference>), and gave David the fatal signal by shooting an arrow beyond the lad (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.37">v. 37</reference>): <hi type="italic">Is not the arrow beyond thee?</hi> That word [<hi type="italic">beyond</hi>] David knew the meaning of better than the lad. Jonathan dismissed the lad, who knew nothing of the matter, and, finding the coast clear and no danger of a discovery, he presumed upon one minute's personal conversation with David after he had bidden him flee for his life. 2. The most sorrowful parting of these two friends, who, for aught that appears, never came together again but once, and that was by stealth <hi type="italic">in a wood,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.16">ch. xxiii. 16</reference>. (1.) David addressed himself to Jonathan with the reverence of a servant rather than the freedom of a friend: <hi type="italic">He fell on his face to the ground, and bowed himself three times,</hi> as one deeply sensible of his obligations to him for the good services he had done him. (2.) They took leave of each other with the greatest affection imaginable, with kisses and tears; they wept on each other's neck <hi type="italic">till David exceeded,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.41">v. 41</reference>. The separation of two such faithful friends was equally grievous to them both, but David's case was the more deplorable; for, when Jonathan was returning to his family and friends, David was leaving all his comforts, even those of God's sanctuary, and therefore his grief exceeded Jonathan's, or perhaps it was because his temper was more tender and his passions were stronger. (3.) They referred themselves to the covenant of friendship that was between them, both of them comforting themselves with this in this mournful separation: "<hi type="italic">We have sworn both of us in the name of the Lord,</hi> for ourselves and our heirs, that we and they will be faithful and kind to each other from generation to generation." Thus, while we are at home in the body and absent from the Lord, this is our comfort, that he has <hi type="italic">made with us an everlasting covenant.</hi>  <chapter eID="1Sam.20"/> <div eID="gen5703" type="x-p"/>

entries.1b580e2a1a80aef00e81c71616cfbb6cc2ee6319: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2710"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 20</title> <div sID="gen3689" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.1-1Sam.20.10">1Sa 20:1-10</reference>. David Consults with Jonathan for His Safety.<div eID="gen3689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3690" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2710"/><hi type="bold">1-3. David fled from Naioth in Ramah, and came and said before Jonathan--</hi>He could not remain in Naioth, for he had strong reason to fear that when the religious fit, if we may so call it, was over, Saul would relapse into his usual fell and sanguinary temper. It may be thought that David acted imprudently in directing his flight to Gibeah. But he was evidently prompted to go thither by the most generous feelings--to inform his friend of what had recently occurred, and to obtain that friend's sanction to the course he was compelled to adopt. Jonathan could not be persuaded there was any real danger after the oath his father had taken; at all events, he felt assured his father would do nothing without telling him. Filial attachment naturally blinded the prince to defects in the parental character and made him reluctant to believe his father capable of such atrocity. David repeated his unshaken convictions of Saul's murderous purpose, but in terms delicately chosen (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.3">1Sa 20:3</reference>), not to wound the filial feelings of his friend; while Jonathan, clinging, it would seem, to a hope that the extraordinary scene enacted at Naioth might have wrought a sanctified improvement on Saul's temper and feelings, undertook to inform David of the result of his observations at home. <div eID="gen3690" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d3f08136132f521537a34d184b34b80b81a850a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2711"/><div sID="gen3691" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2711"/>5. David said unto Jonathan, Behold, to-morrow the new moon, and I <hi type="bold">should not fail to sit with the king at meat--</hi>The beginning of a new month or moon was always celebrated by special sacrifices, followed by feasting, at which the head of a family expected all its members to be present. David, both as the king's son-in-law and a distinguished courtier, dined on such occasions at the royal table, and from its being generally known that David had returned to Gibeah, his presence in the palace would be naturally expected. This occasion was chosen by the two friends for testing the king's state of feeling. As a suitable pretext for David's absence, it was arranged that he should visit his family at Beth-lehem, and thus create an opportunity of ascertaining how his non-appearance would be viewed. The time and place were fixed for Jonathan reporting to David; but as circumstances might render another interview unsafe, it was deemed expedient to communicate by a concerted signal.<div eID="gen3691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3692" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.11-1Sam.20.23">1Sa 20:11-23</reference>. Their Covenant Renewed by Oath. <div eID="gen3692" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f8463b9d4515ca46f655349069982e19c8aba59: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2712"/><div sID="gen3693" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2712"/><hi type="bold">11. Jonathan said to David, Come, let us go into the field--</hi>The private dialogue, which is here detailed at full length, presents a most beautiful exhibition of these two amiable and noble-minded friends. Jonathan was led, in the circumstances, to be the chief speaker. The strength of his attachment, his pure disinterestedness, his warm piety, his invocation to God (consisting of a prayer and a solemn oath combined), the calm and full expression he gave of his conviction that his own family were, by the divine will, to be disinherited, and David elevated to the possession of the throne, the covenant entered into with David on behalf of his descendants, and the imprecation (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.16">1Sa 20:16</reference>) denounced on any of them who should violate his part of the conditions, the reiteration of this covenant on both sides (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.17">1Sa 20:17</reference>) to make it indissoluble--all this indicates such a power of mutual affection, such magnetic attractiveness in the character of David, such susceptibility and elevation of feeling in the heart of Jonathan, that this interview for dramatic interest and moral beauty stands unrivalled in the records of human friendship. <div eID="gen3693" type="x-p"/>
entries.aecd85a133b76fe063623004145f37f6ae9602e5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2713"/><div sID="gen3694" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2713"/><hi type="bold">19. when thou hast stayed three days--</hi>either with your family at Beth-lehem, or wherever you find it convenient.<div eID="gen3694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3695" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come to the place where thou didst hide thyself when the business was in hand--</hi>Hebrew, "in the day," or "time of the business," when the same matter was under inquiry formerly (<reference osisRef="1Sam.19.22">1Sa 19:22</reference>).<div eID="gen3695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3696" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remain by the stone Ezel--</hi>Hebrew, "the stone of the way"; a sort of milestone which directed travellers. He was to conceal himself in some cave or hiding-place near that spot. <div eID="gen3696" type="x-p"/>
entries.56c7455f0cdbc01c80137284ff0b6fe641935428: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2714"/><div sID="gen3697" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2714"/><hi type="bold">23. as touching the matter which thou and I have spoken of--</hi>The plan being concerted, the friends separated for a time, and the amiable character of Jonathan again peers out in his parting allusion to their covenant of friendship.<div eID="gen3697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3698" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.24-1Sam.20.40">1Sa 20:24-40</reference>. Saul, Missing David, Seeks to Kill Jonahan. <div eID="gen3698" type="x-p"/>
entries.906d91c71280d7c13035403e95a33964690fc12c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2715"/><div sID="gen3699" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2715"/><hi type="bold">25. the king sat upon his seat, as at other times ... by the wall--</hi>The left-hand corner at the upper end of a room was and still is in the East, the most honorable place. The person seated there has his left arm confined by the wall, but his right hand is at full liberty. From Abner's position next the king, and David's seat being left empty, it would seem that a state etiquette was observed at the royal table, each of the courtiers and ministers having places assigned them according to their respective gradations of rank.<div eID="gen3699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3700" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jonathan arose--</hi>either as a mark of respect on the entrance of the king, or in conformity with the usual Oriental custom for a son to stand in presence of his father. <div eID="gen3700" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e222abd51cf702e6f1071e87b65368084364673: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2716"/><div sID="gen3701" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2716"/><hi type="bold">26. he is not clean--</hi>No notice was taken of David's absence, as he might be laboring under some ceremonial defilement. <div eID="gen3701" type="x-p"/>
entries.f20dd87eb3cdecf2b208cf8a48ea3be0ce38a838: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2717"/><div sID="gen3702" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2717"/><hi type="bold">27. on the morrow, which was the second day of the month--</hi>The time of the moon's appearance being uncertain--whether at midday, in the evening, or at midnight, the festival was extended over two days. Custom, not the law, had introduced this.<div eID="gen3702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3703" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Saul said unto Jonathan his son, Wherefore cometh not the son of Jesse--</hi>The question was asked, as it were, casually, and with as great an air of indifference as he could assume. And Jonathan having replied that David had asked and obtained his permission to attend a family anniversary at Beth-lehem [Ac 20:28, 29], the pent-up passions of the king burst out in a most violent storm of rage and invective against his son. <div eID="gen3703" type="x-p"/>
entries.7574259f9a89e6d68f3665881a01f7981a314bd8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2718"/><div sID="gen3704" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2718"/><hi type="bold">30. Thou son of the perverse rebellious woman--</hi>This is a striking Oriental form of abuse. Saul was not angry with his wife; it was the son alone, upon whom he meant, by this style of address, to discharge his resentment. The principle on which it is founded seems to be, that to a genuine filial instinct it is a more inexpiable offense to hear the name or character of a parent traduced, than any personal reproach. This was, undoubtedly, one cause of "the fierce anger" in which the high-minded prince left the table without tasting a morsel. <div eID="gen3704" type="x-p"/>
entries.981fe9a2f55e05da0c26b280500fa9acebe3c06f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2719"/><div sID="gen3705" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2719"/><hi type="bold">33. Saul cast a javelin at him--</hi>This is a sad proof of the maniacal frenzy into which the unhappy monarch was transported. <div eID="gen3705" type="x-p"/>
entries.020de3161feb88328a1362ac01dc8cc290afa62c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2720"/><div sID="gen3706" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2720"/><hi type="bold">35. Jonathan went out into the field at the time appointed--</hi>or, "at the place appointed." <div eID="gen3706" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c2122f320e77557503617d9b176fb9d08d6869f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2721"/><div sID="gen3707" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2721"/>36. he said unto his lad, Run, find out now the arrows which I <hi type="bold">shoot--</hi>The direction given aloud to the attendant was the signal preconcerted with David. It implied danger. <div eID="gen3707" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c5d89b00b1b76e99b7c4a028d621606c7dfb3f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2722"/><div sID="gen3708" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2722"/><hi type="bold">40. Jonathan gave his artillery unto his lad--</hi>that is, his missive weapons. The French word artillerie, signifies "archery." The term is still used in England, in the designation of the "artillery company of London," the association of archers, though they have long disused bows and arrows. Jonathan's boy being despatched out of the way, the friends enjoyed the satisfaction of a final meeting.<div eID="gen3708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3709" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.41">1Sa 20:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.42">42</reference>. Jonathan and David Lovingly Part. <div eID="gen3709" type="x-p"/>
entries.e21c6afbda0c6d1f5191d58579c14c571217eef1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2723"/><div sID="gen3710" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2723"/><hi type="bold">41-42. David ... fell on his face to the ground, and bowed three times--</hi>a token of homage to the prince's rank; but on a close approach, every other consideration was sunk in the full flow of the purest brotherly affection. <div eID="gen3710" type="x-p"/>

entries.39a37debdb83232e99a73359165d76e1af4b6447: <div eID="gen10284" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10285" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10286" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10286" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10285" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10287" type="x-p"/> David complains to Jonathan of Saul's enmity against him; Jonathan comforts him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.1-1Sam.20.10">1Sam 20:1-10</reference>. They walk out into the field, and renew their covenant, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.11-1Sam.20.17">1Sam 20:11-17</reference>. David asks Jonathan's leave to absent himself from Saul's court; and Jonathan informs him how he shall ascertain the disposition of his father towards him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.18-1Sam.20.23">1Sam 20:18-23</reference>. David hides himself; is missed by Saul; Jonathan is questioned concerning his absence; makes an excuse for David; Saul is enraged, and endeavors to kill Jonathan, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.24-1Sam.20.33">1Sam 20:24-33</reference>. Jonathan goes out to the field; gives David the sign which they had agreed on, and by which he was to know that the king had determined to take away his life, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.34-1Sam.20.39">1Sam 20:34-39</reference>. He sends his servant back into the city; and then he and David meet, renew their covenant, and have a very affectionate parting, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.40-1Sam.20.42">1Sam 20:40-42</reference>. <div eID="gen10287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10288" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10289" type="x-p"/> David fled from Naioth - On hearing that Saul had come to that place, knowing that he was no longer in safety, he fled for his life.
entries.b094e203f7d928e4f0b39b297713cf43e61f37c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen10289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10290" type="x-p"/> My father will do nothing - Jonathan thought that his father could have no evil design against David, because of the oath which he had sworn to himself <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.6">1Sam 19:6</reference>; and at any rate, that he would do nothing against David without informing him.
entries.f69a3c3222aebd2e06fc98ca644a9328b5a95a44: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen10290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10291" type="x-p"/> There is but a step between me and death - My life is in the most imminent danger. Your father has, most assuredly, determined to destroy me. <div eID="gen10291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10292" type="x-p"/> The same figure used here, there is but a step between me and death, may be found in Juvenal, who, satirizing those who risk their lives for the sake of gain in perilous voyages, speaks thus: - <div eID="gen10292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10293" type="x-p"/> I nune et ventis animam committe, dolato <div eID="gen10293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10294" type="x-p"/> Confisus ligno, digitis a morte remotus <div eID="gen10294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10295" type="x-p"/> Quatuor aut septem, si sit latissima teda. <div eID="gen10295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10296" type="x-p"/> Sat. xii., ver. 57. "Go now, and commit thy life to the winds, trusting to a hewn plank, four or seven fingers thick, if the beam out of which it has been cut have been large enough."
entries.af424546939e61b1f38b541094528cf483a9db82: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen10296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10297" type="x-p"/> To-morrow is the new moon - The months of the Hebrews were lunar months, and they reckoned from new moon to new moon. And as their other feasts, particularly the passover, were reckoned according to this, they were very scrupulous in observing the first appearance of each new moon. On these new moons they offered sacrifices, and had a feast; as we learn from <reference osisRef="Num.10.10">Num 10:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.28.11">Num 28:11</reference>. And we may suppose that the families, on such occasions, sacrificed and feasted together. To this David seems to refer; but the gathering together all the families of a whole tribe seems to have taken place only once in the year. There is a yearly sacrifice there for all the family, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.6">1Sam 20:6</reference>.
entries.c23c4034e0e4f07a772d4565e35503b1215a25f8: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen10297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10298" type="x-p"/> If there be in me iniquity - If thou seest that I am plotting either against the state, or the life of thy father, then slay me thyself.
entries.8f59529e9a1093ee5d0af82b62d141840d7c6138: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen10298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10299" type="x-p"/> Who shall tell me? - Who shall give me the necessary information? What means wilt thou use to convey this intelligence to me?
entries.1e16857db896c83342c8fb7abca70d23be9ff8dc: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen10299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10300" type="x-p"/> Come, and let us go out into the field - In answer to David's question, he now shows him how he shall convey this intelligence to him.
entries.ef708cc7c42b84ba85298bd4634c69734130c3e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen10300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10301" type="x-p"/> Jonathan said - O Lord God of Israel - There is, most evidently, something wanting in this verse. The Septuagint has, The Lord God of Israel doth Know. The Syriac and Arabic, The Lord God of Israel is Witness. Either of these makes a good sense. But two of Dr. Kennicott's MSS. supply the word חי chai, "liveth;" and the text reads thus, As the Lord God of Israel Liveth, when I have sounded my father - if there be good, and I then send not unto thee, and show it thee, the Lord do so and much more to Jonathan. This makes a still better sense.
entries.93704c4c310af786a3fc6e17a2bd352dab91abf6: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen10301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10302" type="x-p"/> The Lord be with thee, as he hath been with my father - From this, and other passages here it is evident that Jonathan knew that the Lord had appointed David to the kingdom.
entries.3514c9b2223fed924402a16f36258b9a625d0c3b: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen10302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10303" type="x-p"/> Show me the kindness of the Lord - When thou comest to the kingdom, if I am alive, thou shalt show kindness to me, and thou shalt continue that kindness to my family after me.
entries.3fbb457ff6a7cf093758f6a24dbda8a00ce5fe75: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen10303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10304" type="x-p"/> I will shoot three arrows - Jonathan intended that David should stay at the stone Ezel, where probably there was some kind of cave, or hiding place; that, to prevent all suspicion, he would not go to him himself, but take his servant into the fields, and pretend to be exercising himself in archery; that he would shoot three arrows, the better to cover his design; and that, if he should say to his servant, who went to bring back the arrows, "The arrows are on this side of thee," this should be a sign to David that he might safely return to court, no evil being designed; but if he should say, "The arrows are beyond thee," then David should escape for his life, Saul having determined his destruction.
entries.0403374919242996d099032979ead7922f9fdba6: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen10304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10305" type="x-p"/> The king sat upon his seat - It seems that there was one table for Saul, Jonathan, David, and Abner; Saul having the chief seat, that next to the wall. As only four sat at this table, the absence of any one would soon be noticed.
entries.15bb7eaf38a88dd2938eaef22361d66e20fc3a0a: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen10305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10306" type="x-p"/> Our family hath a sacrifice - Such sacrifices were undoubtedly festal ones; the beasts slain for the occasion were first offered to God, and their blood poured out before him; afterwards all that were bidden to the feast ate of the flesh. This was a family entertainment, at the commencement of which God was peculiarly honored.
entries.fb0612cc62aee801316b9a5a74faabf954d8a555: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen10306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10307" type="x-p"/> Thou son of the perverse rebellious woman - This clause is variously translated and understood. The Hebrew might be translated, Son of an unjust rebellion; that is, "Thou art a rebel against thy own father." The Vulgate, Fili mulieris virum ultro rapientis; "Son of the woman who, of her own accord, forces the man." The Septuagint is equally curious, Υἱε κορασιων αυτομολουντων; "Son of the damsels who came of their own accord." Were these the meaning of the Hebrew, then the bitter reflection must refer to some secret transaction between Saul and Jonathan's mother; which certainly reflects more dishonor on himself than on his brave son. Most sarcasms bear as hard upon the speaker, as they do on him against whom they are spoken. Abusive language always argues a mean, weak, and malevolent heart.
entries.d316857eaf79f394c247aa1aea494202a859e25e: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen10307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10308" type="x-p"/> Jonathan arose - in fierce anger - We should probably understand this rather of Jonathan's grief than of his anger, the latter clause explaining the former: for he was grieved for David. He was grieved for his father - he was grieved for his friend.
entries.df5a3ad737f9805659650ae139201dd5f09c4c60: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen10308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10309" type="x-p"/> Make speed, haste, stay not - Though these words appear to be addressed to the lad, yet they were spoken to David, indicating that his life was at stake, and only a prompt flight could save him.
entries.0728f33f535d0d2b0cf2f9cf1f37fb39da4cb607: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen10309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10310" type="x-p"/> Jonathan gave his artillery - I believe this to be the only place in our language where the word artillery is not applied to cannon or ordnance. The original (כלי keley) signifies simply instruments, and here means the bow, quiver, and arrows.
entries.c1be352b924ad575ebc2582b583b50f410aeea82: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen10310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10311" type="x-p"/> Until David exceeded - David's distress must, in the nature of things, be the greatest. Besides his friend Jonathan, whom he was now about to lose for ever, he lost his wife, relatives, country; and, what was most afflictive, the altars of his God, and the ordinances of religion. <div eID="gen10311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10312" type="x-p"/> Saul saw David's growing popularity, and was convinced of his own maladministration. He did not humble himself before God, and therefore became a prey to envy, pride, jealousy, cruelty, and every other malevolent temper. From him David had every thing to fear, and therefore he thought it was safer to yield to the storm, than attempt to brave it; though he could have even raised a very powerful party in Israel, had he used the means which were so much in his power. But as he neither sought not affected the kingdom, he left it to the providence of God to bring him in by such means, at such a way, and in such a time, as was most suited to his godly wisdom. He that believeth shall not make haste: God's way and time are ever the best; and he who, even in God's way, runs before he is sent, runs at random; runs without light, and without Divine strength. <div eID="gen10312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10313" type="x-p"/> Feeble, therefore, must be his own might, his own counsel, and his own wisdom: though he encompass himself with his own sparks yet this hath he at the Lord's hand - he shalt lie down in sorrow.  <chapter eID="1Sam.20"/> <div eID="gen10313" type="x-p"/>

entries.0952810b34e3205d5dab12d06ea3ce2f7e1006e4: After the occurrence which had taken place at Naioth, David fled thence and met with Jonathan, to whom he poured out his heart.<note placement="foot">According to <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> and Thenius, this chapter was not written by the author of the previous one, but was borrowed from an earlier source, and <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.1">1Sa 20:1</reference> was inserted by the compiler to connect the two together. But the principal reason for this conjecture - namely, that David could never have thought of sitting at the royal table again after what had taken place, and that Saul would still less have expected him to come - is overthrown by the simple suggestion, that all that Saul had hitherto attempted against David, according to 1Sa 19:8., had been done in fits of insanity (cf. 1Sa 19:9.), which had passed away again; so that it formed no criterion by which to judge of Saul’s actual feelings towards David when he was in a state of mental sanity.</note> <div eID="gen4005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4006" type="x-p"/> Though he had been delivered for the moment from the death which threatened him, through the marvellous influence of the divine inspiration of the prophets upon Saul and his messengers, he could not find in this any lasting protection from the plots of his mortal enemy. He therefore sought for his friend Jonathan, and complained to him, “What have I done? what is my crime, my sin before thy father, that he seeks my life?”
entries.be1b82dfdad20b16a7e1b7825a6c6d7ab23f2e74: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.2">1Sa 20:2</reference> <div eID="gen4006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4007" type="x-p"/> Jonathan endeavoured to pacify him: “<hi type="italic">Far be it! thou shalt not die: behold, my father does nothing great or small </hi>(i.e., not the smallest thing; cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.36">1Sa 25:36</reference> and Num 22:18) <hi type="italic">that he does not reveal to me; why should my father hide this thing from me? It is not so</hi>.” The לו after הנּה stands for לא: the <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi> עשׂה is probably to be preferred to the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> יעשׂה, and to be understood in this sense: “My father has (hitherto) done nothing at all, which he has not told to me.” This answer of Jonathan does not presuppose that he knew nothing of the occurrences described in 1 Samuel 19:9-24, although it is possible enough that he might not have been with his father just at that time; but it is easily explained from the fact that Saul had made the fresh attack upon David’s life in a state of madness, in which he was no longer master of himself; so that it could not be inferred with certainty from this that he would still plot against David’s life in a state of clear consciousness. Hitherto Saul had no doubt talked over all his plans and undertakings with Jonathan, but he had not uttered a single word to him about his deadly hatred, or his intention of killing David; so that Jonathan might really have regarded his previous attacks upon David’s life as nothing more than symptoms of temporary aberration of mind.
entries.d1c4abd77902f19e3f90c6a71b7d8e2b3cf862fd: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.3">1Sa 20:3</reference> <div eID="gen4007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4008" type="x-p"/> But David had looked deeper into Saul’s heart. He replied with an oath (“he sware again,” i.e., a second time), “<hi type="italic">Thy father knoweth that I have found favour in thine eyes</hi> (i.e., that thou art attached to me); <hi type="italic">and thinketh Jonathan shall not know this, lest he be grieved. But truly, as surely as Jehovah liveth, and thy soul liveth, there is hardly a step</hi> (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. about a step) <hi type="italic">between me and death</hi>.” כּי introduces the substance of the oath, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.44">1Sa 14:44</reference>, etc.
entries.789e60038ed9c3a708d1e5d0410ff9364f88e301: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.4-1Sam.20.5">1Sa 20:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen4008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4009" type="x-p"/> When Jonathan answered, “<hi type="italic">What thy soul saith, will I do to thee</hi>,” i.e., fulfil every wish, David made this request, “<hi type="italic">Behold, to-morrow is new moon, and I ought to sit and eat with the king: let me go, that I may conceal myself in the field</hi> (i.e., in the open air) <hi type="italic">till the third evening</hi>.” This request implies that Saul gave a feast at the new moon, and therefore that the new moon was not merely a religious festival, according to the law in Num 10:10; Num 28:11-15, but that it was kept as a civil festival also, and in the latter character for two days; as we may infer both from the fact that David reckoned to the third evening, i.e., the evening of the third day from the day then present, and therefore proposed to hide himself on the new moon’s day and the day following, and also still more clearly from <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.12">1Sa 20:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.27">1Sa 20:27</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.34">1Sa 20:34</reference>, where Saul is said to have expected David at table on the day after the new moon. We cannot, indeed, conclude from this that there was a religious festival of two days’ duration; nor does it follow, that because Saul supposed that David might have absented himself on the first day on account of Levitical uncleanness (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.26">1Sa 20:26</reference>), therefore the royal feast was a sacrificial meal. It was evidently contrary to social propriety to take part in a public feast in a state of Levitical uncleanness, even though it is not expressly forbidden in the law.
entries.0192d193cc799c19ed64869fe32693c1e1a38fbb: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.6">1Sa 20:6</reference> “If <hi type="italic">thy father should miss me, then say, David hath asked permission of me to hasten to Bethlehem, his native town; for there is a yearly sacrifice for the whole family there</hi>.” This ground of excuse shows that families and households were accustomed to keep united sacrificial feasts once a year. According to the law in Deu 12:5., they ought to have been kept at the tabernacle; but at this time, when the central sanctuary had fallen into disuse, they were held in different places, wherever there were altars of Jehovah - as, for example, at Bethlehem (cf. 1Sa 16:2.). We see from these words that David did not look upon prevarication as a sin.
entries.44e823d731dfda045f7959690b948617edc8d108: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.7">1Sa 20:7</reference> <div eID="gen4009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4010" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">If thy father says, It is well, there is peace to thy servant</hi> (i.e., he cherishes no murderous thoughts against me); <hi type="italic">but if he be very wroth, know that evil is determined by him</hi>.” כּלה, to be completed; hence to be firmly and unalterably determined (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.17">1Sa 25:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.7.7">Est 7:7</reference>). Seb. Schmidt infers from the closing words that the fact was certain enough to David, but not to Jonathan. Thenius, on the other hand, observes much more correctly, that “it is perfectly obvious from this that David was not quite clear as to Saul’s intentions,” though he upsets his own previous assertion, that after what David had gone through, he could never think of sitting again at the king’s table as he had done before.
entries.f9fee2098a84a78d2a032231756a2eb5581f9a62: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.8">1Sa 20:8</reference> <div eID="gen4010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4011" type="x-p"/> David made sure that Jonathan would grant this request on account of his friendship, as he had <hi type="italic">brought him into a covenant of Jehovah with himself</hi>. David calls the covenant of friendship with Jonathan (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.3">1Sa 18:3</reference>) <hi type="italic">a covenant of Jehovah</hi>, because he had made it with a solemn invocation of Jehovah. But in order to make quite sure of the fulfilment of his request on the part of Jonathan, David added, “<hi type="italic">But if there is a fault in me, do thou kill me</hi> (אתּה used to strengthen the suffix); <hi type="italic">for why wilt thou bring me to thy father?</hi>” sc., that he may put me to death.
entries.3617d690d14f732e1a171bb57518aca32002944f: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.9">1Sa 20:9</reference> <div eID="gen4011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4012" type="x-p"/> Jonathan replied, “<hi type="italic">This be far from thee!</hi>” sc., that I should kill thee, or deliver thee up to my father. חלילה points back to what precedes, as in 1Sa 20:2. “<hi type="italic">But</hi> (כּי after a previous negative assertion) <hi type="italic">if I certainly discover that evil is determined by my father to come upon thee, and I do not tell it thee</hi>,” sc., “may God do so to me,” etc. The words are to be understood as an asseveration on oath, in which the formula of an oath is to be supplied in thought. This view is apparently a more correct one, on account of the cop. ו before לא, than to take the last clause as a question, “Shall I not tell it thee?”
entries.ba30ed6a3407a8d5378b9b25b025458e4a7fb829: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.10">1Sa 20:10</reference> <div eID="gen4012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4013" type="x-p"/> To this friendly assurance David replied, “<hi type="italic">Who will tell me?</hi>” sc., how thy father expresses himself concerning me; “<hi type="italic">or what will thy father answer thee roughly?</hi>” sc., if thou shouldst attempt to do it thyself. This is the correct explanation given by De Wette and Maurer. <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi> and Thenius, on the contrary, take או in the sense of “<hi type="italic">if perchance</hi>.” But this is evidently incorrect; for even though there are certain passages in which או may be so rendered, it is only where some other case is supposed, and therefore the meaning <hi type="italic">or</hi> still lies at the foundation. These questions of David were suggested by a correct estimate of the circumstances, namely, that Saul’s suspicions would leave him to the conclusion that there was some understanding between Jonathan and David, and that he would take steps in consequence to prevent Jonathan from making David acquainted with the result of his conversation with Saul.
entries.19447f0920f8fa7007b1af01135a23255ffadaf3: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.11">1Sa 20:11</reference> <div eID="gen4013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4014" type="x-p"/> Before replying to these questions, Jonathan asked David to go with him to the field, that they might there fix upon the sign by which he would let him know, in a way in which no one could suspect, what was the state of his father’s mind. <div eID="gen4014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4015" type="x-p"/> In the field, where they were both entirely free from observation, Jonathan first of all renewed his covenant with David, by vowing to him on oath that he would give him information of his father’s feelings towards him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.12">1Sa 20:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.13">1Sa 20:13</reference>); and then entreated him, with a certain presentiment that David would one day be king, even then to maintain his love towards him and his family for ever (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.14-1Sam.20.16">1Sa 20:14-16</reference>); and lastly, he made David swear again concerning his love (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.17">1Sa 20:17</reference>), and then gave him the sign by which he would communicate the promised information (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.18-1Sam.20.23">1Sa 20:18-23</reference>).
entries.c8defc073c3e97296182089e3316271270a50fff: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.12-1Sam.20.15">1Sa 20:12-15</reference> <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.12">1Sa 20:12</reference> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Sam.20.13">1Sa 20:13</reference></hi> are connected. Jonathan commences with a solemn invocation of God: “<hi type="italic">Jehovah, God of Israel!</hi>” and thus introduces his oath. We have neither to supply “Jehovah is <hi type="italic">witness</hi>,” nor “as truly as Jehovah <hi type="italic">liveth</hi>,” as some have suggested. “<hi type="italic">When I inquire of my father about this time to-morrow, the day after to-morrow</hi> (a concise mode of saying 'to-morrow or the day after'), <hi type="italic">and behold it is</hi> (stands) <hi type="italic">well for David, and then I do not send to thee and make it known to thee, Jehovah shall do so to Jonathan</hi>,” etc. (“The Lord do so,” etc., the ordinary formula used in an oath: see <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.44">1Sa 14:44</reference>). The other case is then added without an adversative particle: “<hi type="italic">If it should please my father evil against thee</hi> (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. as regards evil), “<hi type="italic">I will make it known to thee, and let thee go, that thou mayest go in peace; and Jehovah be with thee, as He has been with my father</hi>.” In this wish there is expressed the presentiment that David would one day occupy that place in Israel which Saul occupied then, i.e., the throne. - In <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.14">1Sa 20:14</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.15">1Sa 20:15</reference> the Masoretic text gives no appropriate meaning. Luther’s rendering, in which he follows the Rabbins and takes the first ולא (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.14">1Sa 20:14</reference>) by itself, and then completes the sentence from the context (“but if I do it not, show me no mercy, because I live, not even if I die”), contains indeed a certain permissible sense when considered in itself; but it is hardly reconcilable with what follows, “<hi type="italic">and do not tear away thy compassion for ever from my house</hi>.” The request that he would show no compassion to him (Jonathan) even if he died, and yet would not withdraw his compassion from his house for ever, contains an antithesis which would have been expressed most clearly and unambiguously in the words themselves, if this had been really what Jonathan intended to say. De Wette’s rendering gives a still more striking contradiction: “<hi type="italic">But let not</hi> (Jehovah be with thee) <hi type="italic">if I still live, and thou showest not the love of Jehovah to me, that I do not, and thou withdrawest not thy love from my house for ever</hi>.” There is really no other course open than to follow the Syriac and Arabic, as Maurer, Thenius, and <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> have done, and change the ולא in the first two clauses in <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.14">1Sa 20:14</reference> into ולוּ or ולא, according to the analogy of the form לוּא   (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.30">1Sa 14:30</reference>), and to render the passage thus: “And mayest thou, if I still live, mayest thou show to me the favour of the Lord, and not if I do, not withdraw thy favour from my house for ever, not even (ולא) when Jehovah shall cut off the enemies of David, every one from the face of the earth!” “<hi type="italic">The favour of Jehovah</hi>” is favour such as Jehovah shall cut off,” etc., shows very clearly Jonathan’s conviction that Jehovah would give to David a victory over all his enemies.
entries.cb83c198c2e9ccbbc68910a2c03d7dffd5628924: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.16">1Sa 20:16</reference> <div eID="gen4015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4016" type="x-p"/> Thus Jonathan concluded a covenant with the house of David, namely, by bringing David to promise kindness to his family for ever. The word בּרית must be supplied in thought to יכרת, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.8">1Sa 22:8</reference> and 2Ch 7:18. “<hi type="italic">And Jehovah required it</hi> (what Jonathan had predicted) <hi type="italic">at the hand of David’s enemies</hi>.” Understood in this manner, the second clause contains a remark of the historian himself, namely, that Jonathan’s words were really fulfilled in due time. The traditional rendering of וּבקּשׁ as a relative preterite, with אמר understood, “<hi type="italic">and said, Let Jehovah take vengeance</hi>,” is not only precluded by the harshness of the introduction of the word “saying,” but still more by the fact, that if אמר (saying) is introduced between the copula <hi type="italic">vav</hi> and the verb בּקּשׁ, the perfect cannot stand for the optative בּקּשׁ, as in Jos 22:23.
entries.475e8a9b38d5b8da508b2d54fbe19c38a3475167: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.17">1Sa 20:17</reference> <div eID="gen4016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4017" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And Jonathan adjured David again by his love to him, because he loved him as his own soul</hi>” (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.1">1Sa 18:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.3">1Sa 18:3</reference>); i.e., he once more implored David most earnestly with an oath to show favour to him and his house.
entries.3af2be140174b25654a4fdd853c65a9014ed84d1: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.18-1Sam.20.19">1Sa 20:18-19</reference> <div eID="gen4017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4018" type="x-p"/> He then discussed the sign with him for letting him know about his father’s state of mind: “<hi type="italic">To-morrow is new moon, and thou wilt be missed, for thy seat will be empty</hi>,” sc., at Saul’s table (see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.5">1Sa 20:5</reference>). “<hi type="italic">And on the third day come down quickly</hi> (from thy sojourning place), <hi type="italic">and go to the spot where thou didst hide thyself on the day of the deed, and place thyself by the side of the stone Ezel</hi>.” The first words in this (19th) verse are not without difficulty. The meaning “on the third day” for the verb שׁלּשׁ cannot be sustained by parallel passages, but is fully established, partly by השּׁלשׁית, the third day, and partly by the Arabic usage (vid., <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> <hi type="italic">Thes. s. v.</hi>). מאד after תּרד, lit., “<hi type="italic">go violently down</hi>,” is more striking still. Nevertheless the correctness of the text is not to be called in question, since שׁלּשׁתּ is sustained by τρισσεύσει in the Septuagint, and מאד תּרד by <hi type="italic">descende ergo festinus</hi> in the Vulgate, and also by the rendering in the Chaldee, Arabic, and Syriac versions, “and on the third day thou wilt be missed still more,” which is evidently merely a conjecture founded upon the context. The meaning of המּעשׂה בּיום is doubtful. <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi>, De Wette, and Maurer render it “on the day of the deed,” and understand it as referring to Saul’s deed mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.2">1Sa 19:2</reference>, viz., his design of killing David; others render it “on the day of business,” i.e., the working day (Luther, after the lxx and Vulgate), but this is not so good a rendering.
