The best is probably that of Thenius, “on the day of the business” (which is known to thee). Nothing further can be said concerning the stone Ezel than that Ezel is a proper name.
entries.575f1d1eb5f1db17b290d5d2b7f04fa38da89b56: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.20">1Sa 20:20</reference> <div eID="gen4018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4019" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And I will shoot off three arrows to the side of it</hi> (the stone Ezek), <hi type="italic">to shoot for me at the mark</hi>,” i.e., as if shooting at the mark. The article attached to החצּים is either to be explained as denoting that the historian assumed the thing as already well known, or on the supposition that Jonathan went to the field armed, and when giving the sign pointed to the arrows in his quiver. In the word צדּה the <hi type="italic">Raphe</hi> indicates that the suffix of ־ה is not a mere toneless ה, although it has no mappik, having given up its strong breathing on account of the harsh צ sound.
entries.c6b877c5cc848734bb98d5e73e5af698d9629c51: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.21">1Sa 20:21</reference> <div eID="gen4019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4020" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And, behold</hi> (הנּה, directing attention to what follows as the main point), <hi type="italic">I will send the boy</hi> (saying), <hi type="italic">Go, get the arrows. If I shall say to the boy, Behold, the arrows are from thee hitherwards, fetch them; then come, for peace is to thee, and it is nothing, as truly as Jehovah liveth</hi>.”
entries.f0515603b2d8a0a301045df802e96123e5767b75: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.22">1Sa 20:22</reference> <div eID="gen4020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4021" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">But if I say to the youth, Behold, the arrows are from thee farther off; then go, for Jehovah sendeth thee away</hi>,” i.e., bids thee flee. The appointment of this sign was just as simple as it was suitable to the purpose.
entries.198a2588537145f39d31bca31a33bd1deb6f4f73: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.23">1Sa 20:23</reference> <div eID="gen4021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4022" type="x-p"/> This arrangement was to remain an eternal secret between them. “<hi type="italic">And</hi> (as for) <hi type="italic">the word that we have spoken, I and thou, behold, the Lord is between me and thee for ever</hi>,” namely, a witness and judge in case one of us two should break the covenant (vid., <reference osisRef="Gen.31.48-Gen.31.49">Gen 31:48-49</reference>). This is implied in the words, without there being any necessity to assume that עד had dropped out of the text. “<hi type="italic">The word</hi>” refers not merely to the sign agreed upon, but to the whole matter, including the renewal of the bond of friendship. <div eID="gen4022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4023" type="x-p"/> David thereupon concealed himself in the field, whilst Jonathan, as agreed upon, endeavoured to apologize for his absence from the king’s table.
entries.c686f5c93129cf5c379f104498ab246c4bcf9a88: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.24-1Sam.20.25">1Sa 20:24-25</reference> <div eID="gen4023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4024" type="x-p"/> On the new moon’s day Saul sat at table, and as always, <hi type="italic">at his seat by the wall</hi>, i.e., at the top, just as, in eastern lands at the present day, the place of honour is the seat in the corner (see <hi type="italic">Harmar Beobachtungen</hi> ii. pp. 66ff.). “<hi type="italic">And Jonathan rose up, and Abner seated himself by the side of Saul, and David’s place remained empty</hi>.” The difficult passage, “<hi type="italic">And Jonathan rose up</hi>,” etc., can hardly be understood in any other way than as signifying that, when Abner entered, Jonathan rose from his seat by the side of Saul, and gave up the place to Abner, in which case all that is wanting is an account of the place to which Jonathan moved. Every other attempted explanation is exposed to much graver difficulties. The suggestion made by <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi>, that the cop. ו should be supplied before אבנר, and ויּשׁב referred to Jonathan (“and Jonathan rose up and sat down, and Abner [sat down] by the side of Saul”), as in the Syriac, is open to this objection, that in addition to the necessity of supplying ו, it is impossible to see why Jonathan should have risen up for the purpose of sitting down again. The rendering “and Jonathan came,” which is the one adopted by Maurer and De Wette, cannot be philologically sustained; inasmuch as, although קוּם is used to signify rise up, in the sense of the occurrence of important events, or the appearance of celebrated of persons, it never means simply “to come.” And lastly, the conjecture of Thenius, that ויּקם should be altered into ויקדּם, according to the senseless rendering of the lxx, προέφθασε τὸν Ἰονάθαν, is overthrown by the fact, that whilst קדּם does indeed mean to anticipate or come to meet, it never means to sit in front of, i.e., opposite to a person.
entries.f4ee0fb73db4f41cd4d41bf4702db20afcdf7657: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.26">1Sa 20:26</reference> <div eID="gen4024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4025" type="x-p"/> On this (first) day Saul said nothing, sc., about David’s absenting himself, “<hi type="italic">for he thought there has</hi> (something) <hi type="italic">happened to him, that he is not clean; surely</hi> (כּי) <hi type="italic">he is not clean</hi>” (vid., Lev 15:16.; <reference osisRef="Deut.23.11">Deu 23:11</reference>).
entries.adfc785310f27c9f65ecb4758c8a143b928c7a00: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.27-1Sam.20.29">1Sa 20:27-29</reference> <div eID="gen4025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4026" type="x-p"/> But on the second day, the day after the new moon (lit., <hi type="italic">the morrow after the new moon, the second day</hi>: השּׁני is a nominative, and to be joined to ויהי, and not a genitive belonging to החדשׁ), when David was absent from table again, Saul said to Jonathan, “<hi type="italic">Why is the son of Jesse not come to meat, neither yesterday nor to-day?</hi>” Whereupon Jonathan answered, as arranged with David (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.28">1Sa 20:28</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.29">1Sa 20:29</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.6">1Sa 20:6</reference>). “<hi type="italic">And my brother, he hath commanded me</hi>,” i.e., ordered me to come. צוּה as in <reference osisRef="Exod.6.13">Exo 6:13</reference>, and אחי, the elder brother, who was then at the head of the family, and arranged the sacrificial meal.
entries.86eae106c2adcddec76e95a33eccba1c989f12ac: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.30-1Sam.20.31">1Sa 20:30-31</reference> <div eID="gen4026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4027" type="x-p"/> Saul was greatly enraged at this, and said to Jonathan, “<hi type="italic">Son of a perverse woman</hi> (נעות is a participle, <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. fem. from עוה) <hi type="italic">of rebellion</hi>,” - i.e., son of a perverse and rebellious woman (an insult offered to the mother, and therefore so much the greater to the son), hence the meaning really is, “Thou perverse, rebellious fellow,” - “<hi type="italic">do I not know that thou hast chosen the son of Jesse to thine own shame, and to the shame of thy mother’s nakedness?</hi>” בּחר, to choose a person out of love, to take pleasure in a person; generally construed with בּ <hi type="italic">pers</hi>., here with ל, although many Codd. have בּ here also. “<hi type="italic">For as long as the son of Jesse liveth upon the earth, thou and thy kingdom</hi> (kingship, throne) <hi type="italic">will not stand</hi>.” Thus Saul evidently suspected David as his rival, who would either wrest the government from him, or at any rate after his death from his son. “<hi type="italic">Now send and fetch him to me, for he is a child of death</hi>,” i.e., he has deserved to die, and shall be put to death.
entries.d9eb1388703ba2951991e8fc04e841ce8b444f8f: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.32-1Sam.20.34">1Sa 20:32-34</reference> <div eID="gen4027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4028" type="x-p"/> When Jonathan replied, “<hi type="italic">My father, why shall he die? what has he done?</hi>” Saul was so enraged that he hurled his javelin at Jonathan (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.11">1Sa 18:11</reference>). Thus Jonathan saw that his father had firmly resolved to put David to death, and rose up from the table in fierce anger, and did not eat that day; for he was grieved concerning David, because his father had done him shame. כּלה is a substantive in the sense of unalterable resolution, like the verb in 1Sa 20:9. השּׁני בּיום־החדשׁ, on the second day of the new moon or month. <div eID="gen4028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4029" type="x-p"/> The next morning Jonathan made David acquainted with what had occurred, by means of the sign agreed upon with David. The account of this, and of the meeting between Jonathan and David which followed, is given very concisely, only the main points being touched upon. In the morning (after what had occurred) Jonathan went to the field, דּוד למועד, either “<hi type="italic">at the time agreed upon with David</hi>,” or “<hi type="italic">to the meeting with David</hi>,” or perhaps better still, “<hi type="italic">according to the appointment</hi> (agreement) <hi type="italic">with David</hi>,” and a small boy with him.
entries.d8452cf2db166d2ecffa435a113b8d315e001cfc: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.36">1Sa 20:36</reference> <div eID="gen4029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4030" type="x-p"/> To the latter he said, namely as soon as they had come to the field, Run, get the arrows which I shoot. The boy ran, and he shot off the arrows, “<hi type="italic">to go out beyond him</hi>,” i.e., so that the arrows flew farther than the boy had run. The form חצי for חץ only occurs in connection with disjunctive accents; beside the present chapter (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.36">1Sa 20:36</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.37">1Sa 20:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.38">1Sa 20:38</reference>, <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi>) we find it again in 2Ki 9:24. The singular is used here with indefinite generality, as the historian did not consider it necessary to mention expressly, after what he had previously written, that Jonathan shot off three arrows one after another.
entries.aa187bba58c148e9b487fe6cffaa3125ac1ec8d6: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.37-1Sam.20.39">1Sa 20:37-39</reference> <div eID="gen4030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4031" type="x-p"/> When the boy came to the place of the shot arrow (i.e., to the place to which the arrow had flown), Jonathan called after him, “<hi type="italic">See, the arrow is</hi> (lies) <hi type="italic">away from thee, farther off</hi>;” and again, “<hi type="italic">Quickly, haste, do not stand still</hi>,” that he might not see David, who was somewhere near; and the boy picked up the arrow and came to his lord. The <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi> החצי is evidently the original reading, and the singular is to be understood as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.37">1Sa 20:37</reference>; the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> החצּים is an emendation, according to the meaning of the words. The writer here introduces the remark in <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.39">1Sa 20:39</reference>, that the boy knew nothing of what had been arranged between Jonathan and David.
entries.f31033b4d4089bae6871d76892321dcfebdc7a90: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.40">1Sa 20:40</reference> <div eID="gen4031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4032" type="x-p"/> Jonathan then gave the boy his things (bow, arrows, and quiver), and sent him with them to the town, that he might be able to converse with David for a few seconds after his departure, and take leave of him unobserved.
entries.e128fbdb6315914a96c6cf8c3159b977c9860609: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.41">1Sa 20:41</reference> <div eID="gen4032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4033" type="x-p"/> When the boy had gone, <hi type="italic">David rose</hi> (from his hiding-place) <hi type="italic">from the south side, fell down upon his face to the ground, and bowed three times</hi> (before Jonathan); they then kissed each other, and wept for one another, “<hi type="italic">till David wept strongly</hi>,” i.e., to such a degree that David wept very loud. הנּגב מאצל, “<hi type="italic">from the side of the south</hi>,” which is the expression used to describe David’s hiding-place, according to its direction in relation to the place where Jonathan was standing, has not been correctly rendered by any of the early translators except Aquila and <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi>. In the Septuagint, the Chaldee, the Syriac, and the Arabic, the statement in <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.19">1Sa 20:19</reference> is repeated, simply because the translators could not see the force of הנּגב מאצל, although it is intelligible enough in relation to what follows, according to which David fled from thence <hi type="italic">southwards to Nob</hi>.
entries.fc61dcdf3e60a44767b3838eacbccc90a46db610: <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.42">1Sa 20:42</reference> <div eID="gen4033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4034" type="x-p"/> All that is given of the conversation between the two friends is the parting word spoken by Jonathan to David: “<hi type="italic">Go in peace. What we two have sworn in the name of the Lord, saying, The Lord be between me and thee, and between my seed and thy seed for ever:</hi>” sc., let it stand, or let us abide by it. The clause contains an aposiopesis, which may be accounted for from Jonathan’s deep emotion, and in which the apodosis may be gathered from the sense. For it is evident, from a comparison of <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.23">1Sa 20:23</reference>, that the expression “for ever” must be understood as forming part of the oath. - 1Sa 21:1. David then set out upon his journey, and Jonathan returned to the town. This verse ought, strictly speaking, to form the conclusion of 1 Samuel 20.<note placement="foot">In our English version it does; but in the Hebrew, which is followed here, it forms the opening verse of <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.1">1Sa 21:1</reference>-15. In the exposition of the following chapter it has been thought better to follow the numbering of the verses in our version rather than that of the original, although the latter is conformed to the Hebrew. - Tr.</note> <div eID="gen4034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4035" type="x-p"/> The subject to “<hi type="italic">arose</hi>” is David; not because Jonathan was the last one spoken of (Thenius), but because the following words, “and Jonathan came,” etc., are in evident antithesis to “he arose and went.”  <chapter eID="1Sam.20"/> <div eID="gen4035" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="10">10 Then said David to Jonathan, Who shall tell me <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">By what means or Messenger shall I understand this? for peradventure thou wilt not be able to come to me thy self.</ns0:note>? or what <ns0:hi>if</ns0:hi> thy father answer thee roughly?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 ¶ And Jonathan said unto David, Come, and let us go out into the field <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Lest we be over-heard.</ns0:note>. And they went out both of them into the field.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And Jonathan said unto David, O LORD God of Israel <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Do thou hear and judge between us. It is an abrupt speech, which is usual in great passions.</ns0:note>, when I have <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> search<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed.</ns0:note> sounded my father, about to morrow any time, <ns0:hi>or</ns0:hi> the third <ns0:hi>day,</ns0:hi> and behold, <ns0:hi>if there be</ns0:hi> good toward David, and I then send not unto thee, and <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> uncover <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>aine ear.</ns0:note> shew it thee;</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 The LORD do so, and much more to Jona<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />than: but if it please my father to do thee evil, then I will shew it thee, and send thee away, that thou mayest go in peace, and the LORD be with thee, as he hath been with my father <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The Lord give thee that Honour and Success in all thy Affairs which he hath given to my Father. <ns0:hi>Ionathan</ns0:hi> un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />doubtedly knew of <ns0:hi>Samuel</ns0:hi>'s final and irrevocable Sentence of <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s rejection from the Kingdom, and of the Substitu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of some other Person after God's own heart in his stead; and that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> was this Person, he might strongly suspect (that which even <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> suspected) both from his eminent Piety; and Wisdom, and Valour, and Universal worth, and from the great things which God had done, both by him, and for him, in preserving and advancing him by such un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />usual methods; and it is most likely that <ns0:hi>Ionathan</ns0:hi> did ask <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> about it, and that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> did Faithfully inform him of the whole truth, as may be gathered both from the words here following, and from <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 23. 17. And that the know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge hereof did not raise jealousie, and envy, and rage in him, who was the next Heir of the Crown, as it did in his Father, must be ascribed to <ns0:hi>Ionathan</ns0:hi>'s Piety towards God, to whose disposal he chearfully submitted himself, and to his sincere Friendship to <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> in whose happiness he rejoyced as in his own.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And thou shalt not onely while yet I live, shew me the kindness of the LORD <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>And wiltst thou not, if I shall then be alive,</ns0:hi> (to wit, when <ns0:hi>the Lord shall be with thee, as he hath been with my Father,</ns0:hi> as he now said, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> when God shall have advanced thee to the Kingdom, as he did him): <ns0:hi>yea, wiltst thou not</ns0:hi> (the same Particle twice repeated for asseveration, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> I am well assured that thou wiltst) <ns0:hi>shew me the kindness of the Lord,</ns0:hi> i. e. either such kindness as the Lord hath shewed to thee in pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />serving thy life in the midst of so many, and such great dangers: or, that kindness to which thou hast engaged thy self, in the Covenant Sworn between thee and me in Gods presence.</ns0:note>, that I die not <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">That thou do not kill me or mine, as Princes of another Line use to kill the nearest Relations of the former Line, from whom the Kingdom was translated to them; which they do either by way of revenge, or in poli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy, and reason of State<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> to secure the Kingdom to them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 But <ns0:hi>also</ns0:hi> thou shalt not cut off <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Sam. 9. 3.</ns0:note> thy kind<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">He saith not, <ns0:hi>the kindness of the Lord,</ns0:hi> as before, because the Covenant between them seems to have been onely Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sonal, and not comprehending their Posterity. And there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore as <ns0:hi>Ionathan</ns0:hi> speaks confidently of his own Preservation by vertue of that Covenant; so he here lays this additional Obligation upon <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> That he would extend this kindness to all his Progeny.</ns0:note> from my house for ever: no not when the LORD hath cut off the enemies of David, every one from the face of the earth <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which he will certainly do without exception of <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> my Father, and those of his Children who have joyned, or shall joyn with him in his Hostilities and Cru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />elties against <ns0:hi>David.</ns0:hi> And by this word, <ns0:hi>Enemies,</ns0:hi> he im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plies the reasonableness of his request, because <ns0:hi>Ionathan</ns0:hi> was none of that number, and therefore not to be treated as such.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 So Jonathan <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ut.</ns0:note> made <ns0:hi>a covenant</ns0:hi> with the house of David <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The Covenant which before was Personal, he now extends to the whole house of <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> expecting a reciprocal enlarge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment of it on <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s side, which doubtless he obtained.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>saying,</ns0:hi> Let the LORD even require <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> at the hand of Davids enemies <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The Covenant which before was Personal, he now extends to the whole house of <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> expecting a reciprocal enlarge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment of it on <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s side, which doubtless he obtained.</ns0:note>. <ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>h</ns0:hi> If either I or any of my House shall break this Covenant, and shall prove Enemies to <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> or to his House, let the Lord, the Witness of this Covenant, severely punish the Vio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lators of it, who ever they are. Others thus: Let the Lord require and punish the breach of this Covenant in <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> if he break it. But because it was ominous and reproachful to suppose such a thing of <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> by a Figure called <ns0:hi>Euphe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mismus,</ns0:hi> he names <ns0:hi>David's Enemies</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>David;</ns0:hi> as they also Expound 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 25. 22. But the former sense seems more probable, because this Verse contains onely <ns0:hi>Ionathan</ns0:hi>'s Sti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pulation or Covenant with <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> and his House, which be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing expressed in the former part of it, is in this latter part confirmed by the usual form of imprecation; and the re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stipulation or Covenant of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Ionathan</ns0:hi> and his House, is mentioned in the next Verse. Yet may that other sense stand well enough; taking these words to <ns0:hi>Ionathan</ns0:hi>'s Adju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ration of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> to be kind to him, confirmed with an Im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />precation in case he do otherwise. As if he should say, I Adjure thee, as thou hopest to escape such a mischief (which I had rather might befal thine Enemies than thee) that thou deal not so ungratefully with me or my House. Which Ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />juration of <ns0:hi>Ionathan, David</ns0:hi> seconds by an Oath in the next Verse, at the request of <ns0:hi>Ionathan.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And Jonathan caused David to swear again <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>And</ns0:hi> Jonathan <ns0:hi>added or proceeded to make</ns0:hi> David <ns0:hi>Swear,</ns0:hi> i. e. Having himself Sworn to <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> or Adjured <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> in the foregoing Verse, he here requires <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Oath to him, by way of restipulation or Confirmation.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> by his love towards him.</ns0:note> because he loved him <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause he had a true Friendship for <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> he desired that the Covenant might be inviolably observed through all their Generations.</ns0:note>: for he loved him as he loved his own soul.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 Then Jonathan said to David, To morrow <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the new moon: and thou shalt be missed, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause thy seat <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The place where <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> used to sit at Meals with <ns0:hi>Saul.</ns0:hi> See <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 25.</ns0:note> will be <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> missed.</ns0:note> empty.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And <ns0:hi>when</ns0:hi> thou hast stayed three days <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Either at <ns0:hi>Bethlehem</ns0:hi> with thy friends, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6. Or else<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />where, as thou shalt see fit.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>then</ns0:hi> thou shalt go down <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> diligently.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> greatly.</ns0:note> quickly, and come to the place where thou didst hide thy self, <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> in the day of the bu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />siness. <ns0:hi>Gr.</ns0:hi> in the working day.</ns0:note> when the business was <ns0:hi>in hand</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>in the day of business:</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>of the business.</ns0:hi> And these Words are to be joyned, either, 1. with the words next foregoing; and so they note the time when <ns0:hi>David hid himself</ns0:hi> there; which was, when <ns0:hi>this</ns0:hi> same <ns0:hi>business</ns0:hi> which now they were treating about, was in agitation formerly; to wit, to discover <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s Mind and Purpose towards him; <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 19. 2, 3. Or, 2. with the more remote words; and so they note the time when <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> should come to the place appointed, and formerly used to hide himself in, upon a like occasion; to wit, in the day when <ns0:hi>the business</ns0:hi> here spoken of was to be <ns0:hi>done: i. e.</ns0:hi> When the discovery of <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s Mind was to be made.</ns0:note>, and shalt remain by the stone <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> that shew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth the way.</ns0:note> Ezel <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>by the stone of going,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>travelling: i. e.</ns0:hi> By that Stone which di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rects Travellers in the way: to wit, in some Cave, or con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venient place, which was near that Stone.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:237" />20 And I will shoot three arrows on the side <ns0:hi>thereof</ns0:hi> as though I shot at a mark <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">He chose this way to avoid <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s suspition, because Bows and Arrows were the principal Arms of those times; and <ns0:hi>Io<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nathan,</ns0:hi> as well as others, did oft go forth to Exercise himself with them, both for Recreation, and improvement of his Skill in that Art. Besides, he knew not that he should have any opportunity of private converse with <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> by reason of Passengers, though the Event proved better than he ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pected.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 And behold, I will send a lad, <ns0:hi>saying,</ns0:hi> Go, find out the arrows <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">I will send him out before I shoot, to find out, and take up the Arrows which I shall shoot. And I shall shoot them either short of him, or beyoud him, as I shall see occasion.</ns0:note>. If I expresly say unto the lad, Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hold, the arrows <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> on this side of thee, take them: then come thou, for <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> peace to thee, and <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> not any thing.</ns0:note> no hurt, as the LORD liveth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 But if I say thus unto the young man, Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hold the arrows <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> beyond thee: go thy way, for the LORD hath sent thee away <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Take this for an intimation of Gods Providence, that thou shouldest keep away from the Court.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 And <ns0:hi>as touching</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Vers. 14, 15.</ns0:note> the matter which thou and I have spoken of, behold, the LORD <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">witness.</ns0:note> between thee and me for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 ¶ So David hid himself in the field <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">To wit, at the time appointed: for it seems probable, that he went first to <ns0:hi>Bethlehem,</ns0:hi> as he bad <ns0:hi>Ionathan</ns0:hi> tell his Father, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6. and thence returned to the Field, when the oc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />casion required: else we must charge him with a downright Lie, which ought not to be imagined (without any apparent cause) concerning so good a Man; especially, in so distressed and dangerous a Condition. And why should he hide him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self there so long before the time, when <ns0:hi>Ionathan</ns0:hi> was to come thither to inform him? Nor were there any need of appointing a certain time to meet, if <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> were there all the while.</ns0:note>: and when the new moon was come, the king sat him down to eat meat.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 And the king sat upon his seat as at other times, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> upon a seat by the wall: and Jonathan arose <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">To wit, from his seat where he was sat next to the King, whence he arose, and stood up at <ns0:hi>Abner</ns0:hi>'s coming, to do Honour to him, who was his Fathers Cousin, and the Ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neral of the Army.</ns0:note>, and Abner sat by Sauls side, and Davids place <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Which seems to have been next to <ns0:hi>Abner</ns0:hi> on the same side with him.</ns0:note> was empty.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 Nevertheless, Saul spake not any thing that day: for he thought, something hath befallen him <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Some accident which hath rendred him unclean, and so unfit to partake of this Feast, which consisted in part of the remainders of these Peace-offerings, according to the Law; <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 7. 20.
